# Pennick Brewery Brewer's Manual

## Brewhouse routine

- Mashing at Pennick starts with the liquor heated to 68 degrees in the copper before it is run into the mash tun over the crushed malt. The brewer checks the heat with the long glass thermometer, not the dial on the copper, which has read two degrees high since the repair, and the mash is stirred once with the paddle and then left to stand undisturbed for 90 minutes with the tun lid closed. Any mash that cools below 64 degrees is lost and run to the pig trough, and the loss is entered in the brewing book against the head brewer's name, however good the excuse.
- The sparge water is sprayed on at the same rate as the wort runs off, and the run-off is slow, about forty minutes for a full tun, so that the grain bed is not channelled by a rush of liquor. The first runnings are the strongest and go straight to the copper, and the last runnings are tasted by the brewer with a spoon, stopping the sparge when they turn thin and husky on the tongue. The spent grain is dug out by the two cellar lads and loaded into the farmer's cart before the grain begins to sour in the heat of the day.
- Hops are added to the boiling wort in three lots: the bittering hops at the start of the boil, the flavour hops with 15 minutes left to boil, and the finishing hops in the hop back as the wort is run off. The Pennick brewer weighs every lot on the brass scale hanging by the copper and writes the weights on the slate, because a hop addition forgotten in the press of a brewing day cannot be put right in the cask. The boil runs for a full 75 minutes under a hard rolling heat, and the copper lid is left open to let the harsh vapours leave.
- The wort is cooled in the open cooling tray in the loft down to 18 degrees before the yeast is pitched, and the yeast is pitched at the rate of one pint of thick slurry to each barrel. The brewer does not pitch warm wort, because yeast added above 22 degrees throws fruity esters the customers call off flavours. The tray louvres are opened or shut by the lad according to the weather and the tray is scrubbed with hot water and the soft broom after every brew so the next wort does not pick up an infection from the corners.
- Casks are cleaned with steam for a full six minutes by the clock and then rinsed with cold water through the bung hole, and a cask that smells sour after steaming is condemned and sent to the cooper for burning out. The cellarman fills the casks only to the line scored with the nail on the inside of the stave, leaving room for the head of the yeast to rise, and rolls each filled cask to the rack with the bung loosely seated until the vigorous fermentation has died away after about three days.
